claim: Candida albicans is associated with nearly half a million life-threatening infections annually, predominantly in immunocompromised individuals.
source: Candida albicans is the most prevalent human fungal pathogen, associated with nearly half a million life-threatening infections annually, predominantly in immunocompromised individuals (Brown and Netea, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Brown and Netea, 2012.

claim: C. albicans is a heterozygous diploid yeast capable of mating, yet true meiosis has not been observed.
source: C. albicans is a heterozygous diploid yeast capable of mating, yet true meiosis has not been observed.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and represents established knowledge about C. albicans.

claim: C. albicans undergoes a parasexual process that involves random chromosome loss and rare Spo11-dependent chromosome recombination events.
source: Instead, it undergoes a parasexual process that involves random chromosome loss and rare Spo11-dependent chromosome recombination events (Bennett and Johnson, 2003; Forche et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bennett and Johnson, 2003; Forche et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2018.

claim: The majority of genomic diversity observed in C. albicans is attributed to asexual mitotic genome rearrangements.
source: The majority of genomic diversity observed in C. albicans is attributed to asexual mitotic genome rearrangements (Forche et al., 2011; Lephart and Magee, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Forche et al., 2011; Lephart and Magee, 2006.

claim: C. albicans did not undergo an ancient whole genome duplication event like Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
source: Additionally, while C. albicans did not undergo an ancient whole genome duplication event like Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Butler et al., 2009; Marcet-Houben et al., 2009; Wolfe and Shields, 1997), small-scale duplication events have resulted in gene family expansions, especially in sub-telomeric regions (Anderson et al., 2012; Butler et al., 2009; Dunn et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Butler et al., 2009; Marcet-Houben et al., 2009; Wolfe and Shields, 1997.

claim: Small-scale duplication events have resulted in gene family expansions in C. albicans, especially in sub-telomeric regions.
source: Additionally, while C. albicans did not undergo an ancient whole genome duplication event like Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Butler et al., 2009; Marcet-Houben et al., 2009; Wolfe and Shields, 1997), small-scale duplication events have resulted in gene family expansions, especially in sub-telomeric regions (Anderson et al., 2012; Butler et al., 2009; Dunn et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Anderson et al., 2012; Butler et al., 2009; Dunn et al., 2018.

claim: C. albicans has at least three major classes of long repetitive sequences: telomeric repeat units and TLO gene family, Major Repeat Sequences (MRS), and ribosomal DNA repeats (rDNA).
source: First, repeat analysis in C. albicans has characterized at least three major classes of long repetitive sequences: the 23 bp tandem telomeric repeat units and the 14 member telomere-associated (TLO) gene family residing in sub-telomeric regions; the Major Repeat Sequences (MRS) found, at least in part, on every C. albicans chromosome and formed by a long tandem array of ~2.1 kb RPS units flanking non-repetitive HOK and RBP-2 elements (Chibana et al., 1994; Chindamporn et al., 1998; Lephart and Magee, 2006); and the ribosomal DNA repeats (rDNA) found on ChrR, which are organized as a tandem array of up to ~200 copies of ~12 kb units (Freire-Benéitez et al., 2016; Jones et al., 2004; Rustchenko et al., 1993; Wickes et al., 1991).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations describing these repeat classes.

claim: Long repetitive sequences in C. albicans can undergo both inter- and intra-locus recombination events that rapidly generate chromosome length polymorphisms, chimeric chromosomes, and telomere-telomere chromosomal fusions.
source: These long repetitive sequences can undergo both inter- and intra-locus recombination events that rapidly generate chromosome length polymorphisms, chimeric chromosomes, and telomere-telomere chromosomal fusions (Chu et al., 1992; Selmecki et al., 2006; Selmecki et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chu et al., 1992; Selmecki et al., 2006; Selmecki et al., 2010.

claim: The C. albicans genome contains thousands of small chromosomal inversion events (~10 genes long) relative to S. cerevisiae.
source: Over 19 years ago, Wolfe and colleagues showed that the C. albicans genome contains thousands of small chromosomal inversion events (~10 genes long) relative to S. cerevisiae.
evidence: The claim is attributed to work by Wolfe and colleagues from over 19 years ago.

claim: The C. albicans genome had the highest rate of genome instability due to micro- and macro-rearrangements of syntenic gene blocks, relative to 11 other hemiascomycete species.
source: Similarly, Dujon and colleagues demonstrated that the C. albicans genome had the highest rate of genome instability due to micro- and macro-rearrangements of syntenic gene blocks, relative to 11 other hemiascomycete species (Fischer et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fischer et al., 2006.

claim: Rates of LOH increase during exposure to elevated temperature (37°C), DNA transformation, and antifungal drugs.
source: For example, rates of LOH increase during exposure to elevated temperature (37°C), DNA transformation, and antifungal drugs (Bouchonville et al., 2009; Forche et al., 2011; Forche et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bouchonville et al., 2009; Forche et al., 2011; Forche et al., 2018.

claim: LOH is increased during in vivo models of infection.
source: LOH is also increased during in vivo models of infection (Ene et al., 2018; Forche et al., 2008; Forche et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ene et al., 2018; Forche et al., 2008; Forche et al., 2018.

claim: Aneuploidy is found in ~50% of isolates resistant to fluconazole (FLC).
source: For example, aneuploidy is found in ~50% of isolates resistant to the most common antifungal drug, fluconazole (FLC).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text.

claim: The most common and only recurrent aneuploidy in different strain backgrounds is the amplification of the left arm of chromosome 5 (Chr5L), often through acquisition of a novel isochromosome structure (i(5L)).
source: The most common and only recurrent aneuploidy in different strain backgrounds is the amplification of the left arm of chromosome 5 (Chr5L), often through acquisition of a novel isochromosome structure (denoted as i(5L)), comprised of two copies of Chr5L separated by the centromere (Selmecki et al., 2006; Selmecki et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Selmecki et al., 2006; Selmecki et al., 2008.

claim: Acquisition of i(5L) conferred FLC resistance via the amplification of two genes, ERG11 and TAC1.
source: Acquisition of i(5L) conferred FLC resistance via the amplification of two genes, ERG11 and TAC1, encoding the drug target (Erg11) and a transcriptional activator of drug efflux pumps (Tac1) (Selmecki et al., 2008; Selmecki et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Selmecki et al., 2008; Selmecki et al., 2009.

claim: The centromere of Chr5 contains a long inverted repeat sequence, and recombination between these repeats can form homozygous isochromosomes of both the left arm (i(5L)) and right arm of Chr5 (i(5R)).
source: Importantly, the centromere of Chr5 contains a long inverted repeat sequence, and recombination between these repeats can form homozygous isochromosomes of both the left arm (i(5L)) and right arm of Chr5 (i(5R)) (Selmecki et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Selmecki et al., 2006.

claim: Long repeat sequences are involved in the formation of all observed CNV breakpoints and chromosome inversions, and many LOH breakpoints, across 33 diverse clinical and experimentally evolved isolates.
source: We provide evidence that long repeat sequences are involved in the formation of all observed CNV breakpoints and chromosome inversions, and many LOH breakpoints, across 33 diverse clinical and experimentally evolved isolates.
evidence: The claim is a primary finding of the study, supported by data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Long repeats that are associated with genome rearrangements (CNV, LOH, and inversions) have on average higher sequence identity than all long repeats combined.
source: Long repeats that are associated with genome rearrangements (CNV, LOH, and inversions) have on average higher sequence identity than all long repeats combined.
evidence: The claim is a primary finding of the study, supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Long repeats that contain ORFs are longer and associated with more genome rearrangements than long repeats that contain other genomic features.
source: Additionally, long repeats that contain ORFs (including partial ORF sequences, single complete ORF sequences (paralogs), or multiple ORFs and intergenic sequences) are longer and associated with more genome rearrangements than long repeats that contain other genomic features (such as LTRs, retrotransposons, or tRNAs).
evidence: The claim is a primary finding of the study, supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Repeat copies involved in genome rearrangements can be located up to ~1.6 Mb apart on the same chromosome.
source: Additionally, repeat copies involved in genome rearrangements can be located up to ~1.6 Mb apart on the same chromosome, suggesting a non-conventional, long-range mechanism for DNA double-strand break (DSB) repair and somatic genome diversification.
evidence: The claim is a primary finding of the study, supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Isolate AMS3743 had four copies of the right arm of Chr4 (Chr4R), but only two copies of Chr4L, and the copy number breakpoint occurred at the centromere of Chr4 (CEN4).
source: Read depth analysis indicated that this isolate had four copies of the right arm of Chr4 (Chr4R), but only two copies of Chr4L, and the copy number breakpoint occurred at the centromere of Chr4 (CEN4) (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by read depth analysis data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: CEN4 is comprised of a CENP-A-binding core sequence (~3.1 kb) flanked by a long (524 bp) inverted repeat.
source: Wildtype CEN4, like CEN5, is comprised of a CENP-A-binding core sequence (~3.1 kb) flanked by a long (524 bp) inverted repeat (Burrack et al., 2016; Ketel et al., 2009; Sanyal et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Burrack et al., 2016; Ketel et al., 2009; Sanyal et al., 2004.

claim: Isolate AMS3743 had a novel ~1.2 Mb chromosome band that hybridized to a CEN4 probe via Southern blot.
source: Isolate AMS3743 had a novel ~1.2 Mb chromosome band that hybridized to a CEN4 probe via Southern blot (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Southern blot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The ~1.2 Mb band was twice the size of the right arm of Chr4 (~607 Kb).
source: This ~1.2 Mb band was twice the size of the right arm of Chr4 (~607 Kb).
evidence: The claim is based on measurement and comparison of chromosome band sizes.

claim: A single primer amplified a ~4.1 kb product from Chr4R through CEN4 and back to Chr4R in the isolate with i(4R) but did not amplify any sequence in the reference (SC5314) or progenitor (P78042) isolates.
source: Consistent with an isochromosome i(4R) structure (a centromere flanked by inverted copies of Chr4R), a single primer amplified a ~4.1 kb product, from Chr4R through CEN4 and back to Chr4R in the isolate with i(4R) but did not amplify any sequence in the reference (SC5314), or progenitor (P78042) isolates (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by PCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: In the presence of FLC, the i(4R) isolate grew significantly better than the progenitor P78042 (p<0.0006, t-test).
source: In the presence of FLC, the i(4R) isolate grew significantly better than the progenitor P78042 (p<0.0006, t-test, Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 1D with statistical analysis.

claim: In the absence of FLC, the i(4R) isolate grew as well as the progenitor P78042.
source: Interestingly, in the absence of FLC, the i(4R) isolate grew as well as the progenitor P78042 (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: i(4R) was maintained in 12/12 populations for over ~300 generations in the absence of FLC.
source: Furthermore, i(4R) was maintained in 12/12 populations for over ~300 generations in the absence of FLC (see Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data described in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The colony that had lost i(4R) had a reduced growth rate in the presence of FLC, similar to the progenitor P78042.
source: The colony that had lost i(4R) had a reduced growth rate in the presence of FLC, similar to the progenitor P78042 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth curve data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: i(4R) is necessary and sufficient for increased fitness in FLC.
source: Overall, these data imply that the long inverted repeat within CEN4 can generate an independent isochromosome structure comprised of two right arms of Chr4, and that i(4R) is necessary and sufficient for increased fitness in FLC.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that isolates with i(4R) have increased fitness in FLC and isolates that lost i(4R) have reduced fitness.

claim: The CENP-A-binding core sequence of CEN4 contained two different alleles, with one homologue containing a ~3.1 kb sequence inversion between the inverted repeat associated with CEN4.
source: During our investigation of the i(4R) structure, we unveiled a surprising feature of CEN4: the CENP-A-binding core sequence of CEN4 contained two different alleles. One homologue of Chr4 contained a ~3.1 kb sequence inversion between the inverted repeat associated with CEN4.
evidence: The claim is based on observations made during the investigation of i(4R).

claim: The new, inverted CEN4 sequence was detected by PCR in the reference isolate SC5314, and in the distantly related isolates P78042 and AMS3743.
source: The new, inverted CEN4 sequence was detected by PCR in the reference isolate SC5314, and in the distantly related isolates P78042 and AMS3743 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C & D).
evidence: The claim is supported by PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C & D.

claim: Sanger sequencing indicated that a recombination event occurred between the two arms of the inverted repeat.
source: Sanger sequencing indicated that a recombination event occurred between the two arms of the inverted repeat (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by Sanger sequencing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: 1974 long repeat matches were identified after excluding all rDNA, MRS and sub-telomeric repeat sequences.
source: After excluding all rDNA, MRS and sub-telomeric repeat sequences, 1974 long repeat matches were identified (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is based on bioinformatic analysis using MUMmer.

claim: The remaining long repeat sequences cover 2.87% of the haploid reference genome.
source: The remaining long repeat sequences cover 2.87% of the haploid reference genome (see Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is based on calculation from the bioinformatic analysis.

claim: The number of all repeat matches per chromosome was correlated with chromosome size (R2 = 0.65, p<0.016).
source: The number of all repeat matches per chromosome was correlated with chromosome size (R2 = 0.65, p<0.016, Figure 2B)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Repeat density did not correlate with GC content (R2 = 0.063, p>0.32) or ORF density (R2 = 0.02, p>0.59) on any chromosome arm.
source: This repeat density did not correlate with GC content (R2 = 0.063, p>0.32) or ORF density (R2 = 0.02, p>0.59) on any chromosome arm (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: All ORFs within a long repeat that were associated with a breakpoint were actively transcribed in the reference isolate SC5314 during growth in rich medium.
source: First, all ORFs within a long repeat that were associated with a breakpoint were indeed actively transcribed in the reference isolate SC5314 during growth in rich medium (Bruno et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bruno et al., 2010.

claim: Spacer length ranged from 1 bp to 2,856,212 bp (median ~82.8 kb, excluding the complex tandem repeat genes).
source: Strikingly, spacer length ranged from 1 bp to 2,856,212 bp (median ~82.8 kb, excluding the complex tandem repeat genes, see Materials and methods)
evidence: The claim is based on bioinformatic analysis of repeat sequences.

claim: Spacer length was correlated with chromosome size (R2 = 0.066, p<0.0001).
source: Strikingly, spacer length ranged from 1 bp to 2,856,212 bp (median ~82.8 kb, excluding the complex tandem repeat genes, see Materials and methods), and was correlated with chromosome size (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, R2 = 0.066, p<0.0001).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The distribution of spacer lengths was significantly different between chromosomes (p<0.035, Kruskal-Wallis with Dunn's multiple comparison test).
source: Additionally, the distribution of spacer lengths was significantly different between chromosomes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B, p<0.035, Kruskal-Wallis with Dunn's multiple comparison test)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The most common long repeats contained lone long terminal repeats (LTRs) (775), followed by ORFs (339, excluding the complex tandem repeat genes), tRNAs (334), and retrotransposons (40).
source: The most common long repeats contained lone long terminal repeats (LTRs) (775), followed by ORFs (339, excluding the complex tandem repeat genes), tRNAs (334), and retrotransposons (40).
evidence: The claim is based on annotation of long repeat sequences.

claim: LTR matched repeat pairs were predominantly dispersed on different chromosomes (78%), while ORF matched repeat pairs were predominantly located on a single chromosome (64%).
source: Interestingly, LTR matched repeat pairs were predominantly dispersed on different chromosomes (78%), while ORF matched repeat pairs were predominantly located on a single chromosome (64%, Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Long repeat sequences containing ORFs had the lowest median sequence identity when compared to repeats containing other features (p<0.0001, Kruskal-Wallis with Dunn's multiple comparison test).
source: Of the matched repeat pairs, the long repeat sequences containing ORFs had the lowest median sequence identity when compared to repeats containing other features (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A, p<0.0001, Kruskal-Wallis with Dunn's multiple comparison test).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Repeats containing ORFs had significantly longer copy length than any other genomic feature (p<0.0001, Kruskal-Wallis with Dunn's multiple comparison test).
source: Conversely, repeats containing ORFs had significantly longer copy length than any other genomic feature (p<0.0001, Kruskal-Wallis with Dunn's multiple comparison test)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The full-length coding sequence of all ORFs that were contained within long repeat sequences were significantly longer (median value of 1380 bp vs 1200 bp, p<0.0008, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test) than the full-length coding sequence of all ORFs not contained within long repeat sequences.
source: In contrast, the full-length coding sequence of all ORFs that were contained within long repeat sequences, were significantly longer (median value of 1380 bp vs 1200 bp, Figure 2—figure supplement 3D, p<0.0008, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test) and had a significantly higher GC content (median value of 37.22% vs 35.22% Figure 2—figure supplement 3E, p<0.0001, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test) than the full-length coding sequence of all ORFs not contained within long repeat sequences (genome-wide, excluding the complex tandem repeat genes, see Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3D.

claim: The full-length coding sequence of all ORFs that were contained within long repeat sequences had a significantly higher GC content (median value of 37.22% vs 35.22%, p<0.0001, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test) than the full-length coding sequence of all ORFs not contained within long repeat sequences.
source: In contrast, the full-length coding sequence of all ORFs that were contained within long repeat sequences, were significantly longer (median value of 1380 bp vs 1200 bp, Figure 2—figure supplement 3D, p<0.0008, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test) and had a significantly higher GC content (median value of 37.22% vs 35.22% Figure 2—figure supplement 3E, p<0.0001, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test) than the full-length coding sequence of all ORFs not contained within long repeat sequences (genome-wide, excluding the complex tandem repeat genes, see Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3E.

claim: Among the 13 diverse isolates, 19 segmental aneuploidies were confirmed, with at least one segmental aneuploidy detected on each of the eight chromosomes.
source: Among the 13 diverse isolates, 19 segmental aneuploidies were confirmed, with at least one segmental aneuploidy detected on each of the eight chromosomes (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–J).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–J.

claim: Segmental amplifications were more frequent (12/19, 63.2%) than segmental deletions (3/19, 15.8%).
source: Segmental amplifications were more frequent (12/19, 63.2%) than segmental deletions (3/19, 15.8%).
evidence: The claim is based on counting and categorizing segmental aneuploidies.

claim: Every CNV breakpoint occurred within 2 kb of a long repeat sequence, ranging from 248 bp to ~4.76 kb in length.
source: Strikingly, every CNV breakpoint occurred within 2 kb of a long repeat sequence, ranging from 248 bp to ~4.76 kb in length.
evidence: The claim is a primary finding of the study, supported by analysis of CNV breakpoints.

claim: Observed breakpoints had significantly more overlap with long repeat sequences than expected given the total genome coverage of long repeat sequences (p<0.0001, two-tailed Fishers Exact Test).
source: Observed breakpoints had significantly more overlap with long repeat sequences than expected given the total genome coverage of long repeat sequences (p<0.0001, two-tailed Fishers Exact Test, see Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis using Fisher's Exact Test.

claim: Repeats containing ORFs were significantly more common than all other types of repeats at CNV breakpoints (18/26 CNV breakpoints, p<0.001, χ2 Goodness-of-fit test).
source: Importantly, repeats containing ORFs were significantly more common than all other types of repeats at these breakpoints (18/26 CNV breakpoints, p<0.001, χ2 Goodness-of-fit test).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis using χ2 Goodness-of-fit test.

claim: 153 LOH breakpoints were identified in the 20 isolates.
source: 153 LOH breakpoints were identified in the 20 isolates (See Materials and methods, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of LOH breakpoints.

claim: 61/153 LOH breakpoints were found within 2 kb of a long repeat sequence.
source: 61/153 LOH breakpoints were found within 2 kb of a long repeat sequence, and, like the CNV breakpoints, these LOH breakpoints could occur on any chromosome (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The copy length of the repeat sequences found at LOH breakpoints ranged from 78 bp to 6499 bp (median 516 bp) with sequence identities ranging from 82.2% to 100% (median of 95.1%).
source: The copy length of the repeat sequences found at LOH breakpoints ranged from 78 bp to 6499 bp (median 516 bp) with sequence identities ranging from 82.2% to 100% (median of 95.1%).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of repeat sequences at LOH breakpoints.

claim: Most of the repeats associated with LOH breakpoints were intra-chromosomal (46/61), in all three orientations (inverted, mirrored, and tandem), and separated by a distance ranging from 903 bp to ~1.6 Mb (median ~35.3 kb).
source: Most of the repeats associated with LOH breakpoints were intra-chromosomal (46/61), in all three orientations (inverted, mirrored, and tandem), and separated by a distance ranging from 903 bp to ~1.6 Mb (median ~35.3 kb).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of repeat sequences at LOH breakpoints.

claim: The LOH breakpoint in SC5314 on Chr3R occurred in orf19.5880 near an 8 bp sequence (AACTTCTT) identical to part of the C. albicans 23 bp telomere repeat sequence.
source: Remarkably, the LOH breakpoint occurred in orf19.5880 near an 8 bp sequence (AACTTCTT) identical to part of the C. albicans 23 bp telomere repeat sequence (GGTGTACGGATTGTCTAACTTCTT).
evidence: The claim is based on sequence analysis of the LOH breakpoint.

claim: A second copy of the same 8 bp sequence was found in an inverted orientation ~3.4 kb away in the adjacent ORF (orf19.5884).
source: Furthermore, a second copy of this same 8 bp sequence was found in an inverted orientation ~3.4 kb away in the adjacent ORF (orf19.5884).
evidence: The claim is based on sequence analysis.

claim: PCR amplification between unique sequences flanking the inverted repeat revealed a ~32 kb inversion in P75063 and SC5314.
source: PCR amplification between unique sequences flanking the inverted repeat revealed a ~32 kb inversion in P75063 and SC5314 and was the only orientation that amplified by PCR; the reference orientation did not amplify, suggesting that the reference genome may be incorrect at this position (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by PCR data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: All potential inversions had breakpoints within long inverted repeats, and these potentially cause chromosomal inversions of ~4.1 kb to ~102.6 kb in length (median ~39.0 kb).
source: We found that all potential inversions had breakpoints within long inverted repeats, and these potentially cause chromosomal inversions of ~4.1 kb to ~102.6 kb in length (median ~39.0 kb, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: The claim is based on bioinformatic analysis of potential inversions.

claim: Repeats associated with breakpoints (CNV, LOH, and inversion) were significantly longer than all other long repeat sequences (median copy length of 785 bp vs 278 bp, p<0.0001, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test).
source: Repeats associated with breakpoints (CNV, LOH, and inversion) were significantly longer than all other long repeat sequences (median copy length of 785 bp vs 278 bp, p<0.0001, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Repeats associated with breakpoints had a significantly higher percent sequence identity than all other long repeat sequences (median identity of 96.2% vs 94.2%, p<0.036 Kolmogorov-Smirnov test).
source: Repeats associated with breakpoints (CNV, LOH, and inversion) were significantly longer than all other long repeat sequences (median copy length of 785 bp vs 278 bp, p<0.0001, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test), and had a significantly higher percent sequence identity than all other long repeat sequences (median identity of 96.2% vs 94.2%, p<0.036 Kolmogorov-Smirnov test) (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Repeats containing ORFs were the most common repeat identified at breakpoints (33/53, 62.3%).
source: Repeats containing ORFs were longer than repeats containing other genomic features and were the most common repeat identified at breakpoints (33/53, 62.3%, Figure 6B & C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B & C.

claim: Repeats containing ORFs were the only genomic feature with both significantly longer copy length and significantly higher sequence identity at breakpoints than at non-breakpoints (p<0.0001 copy length, p<0.0001 sequence identity Kolmogorov-Smirnov test).
source: Furthermore, repeats containing ORFs were the only genomic feature with both significantly longer copy length and significantly higher sequence identity at breakpoints than at non-breakpoints (p<0.0001 copy length, p<0.0001 sequence identity Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A & B).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A & B.

claim: Nine repeat families were associated with more than one breakpoint type (CNV, LOH, and inversion), and two of these (124 and 151) were associated with all three breakpoint types.
source: Nine repeat families were associated with more than one breakpoint type (CNV, LOH, and inversion), and two of these (124 and 151) were associated with all three breakpoint types.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of repeat families at breakpoints.

claim: Repeat family 124, comprised of 4 ORFs, was one of the longest repeats (~3.2 kb) and had one of the highest percent sequence identities (>99%).
source: Repeat family 124 (Figure 3B and 6A), comprised of 4 ORFs, was one of the longest repeats (~3.2 kb) and had one of the highest percent sequence identities (>99%).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of repeat family 124.

claim: Repeat family 151 flanks CEN4 and was associated with the formation of the novel isochromosome i(4R), which was necessary and sufficient for increased fitness in the presence of FLC.
source: Repeat family 151 flanks CEN4 and was associated with the formation of the novel isochromosome i(4R), which was necessary and sufficient for increased fitness in the presence of FLC (Figure 1C and Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data showing the association of repeat family 151 with i(4R) formation and fitness.

claim: C. albicans centromeres are the earliest firing centers of DNA replication.
source: Notably, C. albicans centromeres are the earliest firing centers of DNA replication (Koren et al., 2010; Tsai et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Koren et al., 2010; Tsai et al., 2014.

claim: Both of the C. albicans centromeres that are flanked by long inverted repeat sequences (CEN4 and CEN5) can form isochromosomes.
source: Both of the C. albicans centromeres that are flanked by long inverted repeat sequences (CEN4 and CEN5) can form isochromosomes (Figure 1 and Selmecki et al., 2006; Selmecki et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 1 and citations to Selmecki et al., 2006; Selmecki et al., 2009.

claim: Acquisition of either isochromosome i(4R) or i(5L) was both necessary and sufficient for increased fitness in the presence of FLC.
source: Acquisition of either isochromosome i(4R) or i(5L) was both necessary and sufficient for increased fitness in the presence of FLC (Figure 1 and Selmecki et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 1 and a citation to Selmecki et al., 2006.

claim: There was no fitness cost associated with either isochromosome in the absence of FLC: i(4R) was stable for ~300 generations in 12/12 populations in the absence of FLC.
source: Additionally, there was no fitness cost associated with either isochromosome in the absence of FLC: i(4R) was stable for ~300 generations in 12/12 populations in the absence of FLC (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The C. albicans CNV and inversion breakpoints are associated with much longer repeat spacer lengths than those described in S. cerevisiae, ranging from ~3.1 kb to ~1.6 Mb (median ~30 kb) and ~3.1 kb to ~94.3 kb (median ~34.6 kb), respectively.

claim: Long repeat sequences found throughout the C. albicans genome are utilized to generate segmental aneuploidies, long-range LOH and sequence inversions.
